title: The farewell sermon, in full
hookLine: at Arafah: your blood and property are sacred, treat women well, all of you are from Adam, and Adam from dust

cards: The plain of Arafah, outside Mecca, on the day of the pilgrimage. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is on what Muslims call the farewell pilgrimage.
Jabir ibn Abdullah, in Sahih Muslim, tells how he rides into the valley and speaks to the people.

His first words tie three sacred things together: your blood and your property are sacred to you, as sacred as this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this city of yours. Today: the farewell sermon.

teach.b: The sermon isn't one document; its lines are spread across the hadith collections, each narrator keeping a part.

Jabir's account keeps his words about women: be mindful of God in how you treat them, for you have taken them on a trust from God. The next day, the day of sacrifice at Mina, Bukhari reports him asking: what day is this?
What month? What city? In Abu Bakrah's report, each time the crowd answers: Allah and His messenger know best.
Then: your blood, your property and your honor are as sacred to one another as this day, in this month, in this city. A sacred day, month and city, laid over every person in front of him.

teach.h: CHILDREN OF ADAM, ADAM FROM DUST.
teach.b: In reports in Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, which some readers gather into the sermon, he says people are all children of Adam, and Adam was made from dust.
No Arab has any merit over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, no light-skinned person over a dark-skinned one, nor the reverse, except by mindfulness of God.
The Qur'an says something close in surah forty-nine: humankind was made into nations and tribes so that they might know one another, and the noblest in God's sight is the most mindful of Him.
In Jabir's account, he asks what they will say of him; they answer that he has conveyed the message. He raises his finger to the sky, points it toward the people, and says: O Allah, bear witness.
And in Bukhari he tells those present to pass it on to those who are absent.
That instruction is part of why you're hearing it now.

how: Muslims read the farewell sermon from the hadith collections, where its parts are spread across several narrations, and it is recited and taught at the time of the hajj and in Friday sermons.

the hill in Mecca where pilgrims walk seven times
the plain where he gave his farewell sermon

games.q: the farewell sermon — tap the pairs.

s: the sermon is kept in one single document
its lines are spread across the hadith collections.
he said no Arab has merit over a non-Arab except by mindfulness of God
in reports in the collection of Ahmad.
in Abu Bakrah's report, the crowd named the day at once
they said: Allah and His messenger know best.

games.q: you're in the crowd on the farewell pilgrimage. the Prophet asks: what day is this? what do you answer?
o: Allah and His messenger know best.
games.why: that was their answer. then he told them: your blood, property and honor are as sacred as this day, in this month, in this city.

practice: If you can, read a translation of the farewell sermon from a reliable source, slowly; if not, hold just three lines: your blood and property are sacred; treat women well, as a trust; all of you are from Adam, and Adam from dust.
Let each one sit for a few breaths, and if you pray, you can ask Allah to help you live by it.

wordCard.voice: Arafah, the plain of his last pilgrimage, where he declared each life and property sacred, and all people from Adam, and Adam from dust. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'the farewell pilgrimage', the name for the Prophet's last hajj.

carryVoice: Your line: all from Adam. The only rank named is mindfulness of God. Day seven hundred ninety-five, done.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 67; 1741 (Abu Bakrah's report of the sermon at Mina: what day is this; sacred as this day; let the present inform the absent)
Sahih Muslim 1218 (Jabir's account of the farewell pilgrimage: the sermon at Arafah, blood and property sacred, women a trust, O Allah bear witness)
Musnad Ahmad 23489; Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3270 (children of Adam, Adam from dust; no Arab over non-Arab)
